extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate and graduate students (and researchers) in combinatorics/graph theory; readers of a combinatorics textbook
extracted.subtask_description: Expository textbook chapters on completing partial Latin squares (Evans conjecture / Smetaniuk proof) and the Dinitz problem (list-coloring the square array) including definitions, lemmas, constructive algorithms, and proofs. Focus is on when a partial Latin square can be completed and on proving that the list-chromatic number of the square graph S_n equals n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial Latin square (definition / admissibility condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A partial Latin square of order n is an n x n array with some cells filled by numbers from {1,...,n} such that every number appears at most once in every row and at most once in every column.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This basic admissibility condition is necessary to have any chance of completing the partial configuration to a full Latin square; it is used repeatedly (e.g., when applying Hall's theorem or permuting rows/columns).

rubrics_metrics.name: Completion existence question (Evans conjecture phrasing)
rubrics_metrics.description: The problem: given a partial Latin square of order n, when can it be completed to a Latin square of the same order?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motivating question for the chapter; special easy cases are discussed (first n-1 rows filled, or only first row filled) to illustrate forced vs many completions and to show that mere small number of filled cells does not guarantee completion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forced completion when first n-1 rows are filled (constructive criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the first n-1 rows are completely filled and the last row is empty, then completion is forced: each symbol appears n-1 times overall and hence is missing from exactly one column; placing each missing symbol in that column yields the unique completion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an immediate constructive method and serves as an example of when a partial Latin square has a unique completion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Many completions when only first row is filled (constructive method)
rubrics_metrics.description: If only the first row is filled, complete the square by cyclically rotating the elements one step in each subsequent row; many completions exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exhibits high freedom when few cells are prefilled; contrasts with forced completion cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conjugacy principle for partial Latin squares
rubrics_metrics.description: Viewing a Latin square as a (3 x n^2) line array with lines R,C,E (rows, columns, elements): any conjugate (permute the three whole lines) of a partial Latin square is again a partial Latin square, and a partial Latin square can be completed iff any conjugate can be completed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle allows one to reformulate the completion problem by permuting the roles of rows, columns and symbols, which is used in reductions in proofs (notably the proof of Lemma 2 and Smetaniuk's theorem).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma (Ryser): extendability of Latin rectangles (r x n) with r < n
rubrics_metrics.description: Any (r x n)-Latin rectangle (first r rows full, r < n) can be extended to an (r+1 x n)-Latin rectangle and hence can be completed to a Latin square.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses Hall's marriage theorem: for column j let A_j be the set of symbols missing from column j; each A_j has size n - r and each symbol is in exactly n - r of the A_j, so Hall's condition holds, giving a system of distinct representatives which forms the next row.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma (Lindner): completion when ≤ n-1 filled cells and ≤ 5 distinct symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: If a partial Latin square of order n has at most n-1 filled cells and involves at most 5 distinct elements (symbols), then it can be completed to a Latin square of order n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof transforms the problem using conjugacy to assume filled entries lie in the top r (<5) rows, orders rows by number of filled cells, and completes rows step-by-step using Hall's theorem on carefully defined sets A_j. Key technical inequalities ensure Hall's condition holds for the constructed family of sets; the argument is delicate and uses bounds on counts of occurrences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smetaniuk's theorem (Evans conjecture solution): completion when ≤ n-1 filled cells
rubrics_metrics.description: Any partial Latin square of order n with at most n-1 filled cells can be completed to a Latin square of the same order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by induction on n. Key steps: find a symbol that occurs only once, permute rows/columns so that all filled cells lie below the diagonal except that unique symbol on the diagonal; remove that symbol and apply induction to the (n-1)-order subproblem; perform a sequence of controlled exchanges to move diagonal elements into the last column (avoiding infinite loops by a bipartite-graph/path argument) and finally fill the first row by Lemma 1. The proof is constructive and yields an explicit completion algorithm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial Latin square non-completability example (counterexample to naive 'fewer than n cells' belief)
rubrics_metrics.description: There exist partial Latin squares with fewer than n filled cells that cannot be completed (explicit small example shown), showing that mere sparsity does not guarantee extendability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use such examples to motivate the necessity of structural conditions and to show the subtlety of the completion problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dinitz problem statement (list-coloring formulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an n x n array where each cell (i,j) is assigned a set C(i,j) of n colors, is it always possible to choose for each cell a color from its set so that colors in every row and every column are distinct? Equivalently: does the list chromatic number x_l(S_n) of the square graph S_n equal n?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relates to Latin squares when all lists are identical; general case is harder because available colors vary by cell. Recasting as a graph list-coloring problem is central to the solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: list coloring and list-chromatic number x_l(G)
rubrics_metrics.description: A list coloring of G assigns to each vertex v a color c(v) in a prescribed list C(v). The list-chromatic number x_l(G) is the smallest k such that for any assignment of lists C(v) with |C(v)| = k there exists a list coloring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This notion generalizes ordinary coloring and is the formal framework for the Dinitz problem. Observe x_l(G) ≥ χ(G) and can be much larger for some graphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma (kernel-based sufficient condition for list coloring)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let D = (V,E) be a directed graph. If for every vertex v we are given a list C(v) with |C(v)| ≥ d^+(v) + 1, and every induced subgraph of D possesses a kernel, then there exists a list coloring choosing for each v a color from C(v).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by induction: pick a color c occurring in some lists, take the induced subgraph A(c) of vertices whose lists contain c; by hypothesis A(c) has a kernel K(c); color all vertices in K(c) with c, delete them and c from remaining lists, observe outdegrees drop appropriately, and continue. The kernel existence is the crucial structural hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: kernel in a directed graph
rubrics_metrics.description: A kernel K ⊆ V in directed graph D=(V,E) is a set satisfying (i) K is independent in the underlying undirected graph (no edges within K), and (ii) for every u ∈ V\, there exists v ∈ K with an arc u -> v.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kernels are the combinatorial objects used in the inductive coloring lemma; existence of kernels in induced subgraphs enables the iterative color-picking procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma (Gale–Shapley): existence of stable matchings in bipartite graphs
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a bipartite graph G=(X ∪ Y, E) with each vertex having a ranking of its neighbors, there always exists a stable matching (no unmatched pair mutually prefer each other over their current partners).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via the deferred-acceptance algorithm: men propose to favorites, women hold best proposal, reject others; iterate until reservoir empty. The produced matching satisfies the stability condition and is used in the kernel existence argument for induced subgraphs of S_n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orientation construction for S_n using a Latin square (to get uniform outdegree n-1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a Latin square L of order n, orient horizontal edges (i,j)--(i,j') from the smaller L(i,j) to the larger L(i,j'), and orient vertical edges (i,j)--(i',j) from the larger to the smaller. With this orientation every vertex (i,j) has outdegree d^+(i,j) = n-1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This orientation is used to apply the kernel-based lemma: lists of size n meet the condition |C(v)| ≥ d^+(v)+1, and the induced-subgraph kernel existence is then obtained via stable matchings in an associated bipartite graph.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem (Galvin): x_l(S_n) = n
rubrics_metrics.description: For every n, the list-chromatic number of the square graph S_n equals n; equivalently, the Dinitz problem has a positive answer: any n x n array of lists of size n admits a choice yielding Latin-square-like distinctness across rows and columns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine the kernel-based list-coloring lemma with the orientation induced by a Latin square and use Lemma on stable matchings to guarantee kernels in all induced subgraphs (via bipartite graph interpretation). The proof is constructive in the sense of giving an orientation and reduction to stable matchings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Line graph / extension remark (criterion for applicability of method)
rubrics_metrics.description: The construction shows S_n is the line graph of the complete bipartite graph K_{n,n}. The method extends to show x_l(H) = χ(H) for line graphs H = L(G) when G is bipartite (i.e., the method works for line graphs of bipartite graphs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This indicates the scope of the technique and highlights a broader conjecture: whether x_l(H)=χ(H) holds for every line graph H remains open. The exposition explains why the bipartite-line-graph case succeeds via the same kernel/stable-matching argument.
